translation:
"If You do not release me, then by the strength of my own ego I cannot become free from the bondage of karma. I am a devotee of the almighty, all-powerful Lord, so no harm can ever befall me — for just as a chaste wife's honor being violated brings shame upon her husband, so the responsibility for my welfare must rest upon You."

Thus the mention of full prostration (sashtang pranam) points us toward surrendering our entire self to the Lord and handing over our whole responsibility to Him — it instructs us to adopt this spirit of taking refuge in God (bhagavad-sharanagati). For the devotee who has taken refuge, wandering through the eighty-four lakh species of life comes to an end. Moreover, verse 56 states that apart from devotion to God, every injunction and prohibition (vidhi-nishedh) is merely a servant of the path of surrender.

_Smartavyah satatam Vishnur, vismartavyah kshane na cha._
_Sarve vidhi-nishedhah syur etayor eva kinkarah. ||56||_
(Vishnu should be remembered always, and never forgotten even for a moment; all injunctions and prohibitions are but servants of these two — remembering Him and never forgetting Him.)

Explaining the sense of this verse, the Samagam says that the Lord's exclusive, single-minded devotees are such that their minds remain fully absorbed in His lotus feet. Not even for a quarter of the time it takes to blink an eye does their attention move away from the Lord's feet. It further says that Vaishnavas are so resolute that they reject the path of ritual injunction, that is, the path of karma. As for what "vidhi" means, the Samagam explains: by vidhi is meant the path of the Vedas, and these Vaishnavas treat this Vedic path as a servant of the path of devotion. Further, of the path of karma laid down by the Vedas, they accept only its essential element — devotion to God — so they regard the path of karma itself as a servant of the path of devotion. A servant is one who is bound to do; whatever work he is told, he does — such a one is his master's own messenger, and such a messenger cannot cause his master trouble. In the same way, the devotee, whose true master is devotion, is not bound to observe rites and rules simply because the Veda's commands of injunction and prohibition tell him so. Its sakhi is given in the Samagam.

_Kabir, Ved hamare het hai, aune ham Vedun ke manhi._
_Auro ku karm bataave, hamku bataave nahi. ||2||_
(Das Kabirji says: the Vedas work for our benefit, and we too, through the Vedas, secure our own welfare.)

This Veda can command people bound by the three gunas to perform karma through its ordinances, but for devotees like us, since it is our servant, it cannot command us to perform karma. Hariram Vyas, in the raga Sarang-Dhanashri, has described what kind of servant the Veda is:

_Shri Vrindavan ke raja Shyam, Radhika taki rani._
_Teen padarath karat majoori, mukti bharat jahan pani._
_Karmi-dharmi karat jevari, gharu chhavat hai gyani._
_Jogi, jati, tapi sannyasi, in chori kai jani._
_Paniha Ved Puran milaniya, kahat sunat yeh bani._
_Ghar-ghar prem-bhakti ki mahima, Vyas sabani pahchani. ||74||_
(Shyam, the King of the abode of Vrindavan, has Radhika as His queen. The three aims of life — artha, dharma, and kama — labor as His hired hands, while liberation itself fetches the water for their toil. All this is described further below.)

The Lord of the abode of Vrindavan is Shri Krishna, and Radhikaji is His queen. The three aims of life — artha, dharma, and kama — labor as servants, working, so to speak, as tradesmen for the Lord's sake, while Liberation performs the lesser task of drawing water to finish their labor. Rites and observances — the mental disciplines of japa, austerity, charity, and pilgrimage-vows — twist the binding rope; and on the roof of the devotees' house the men of knowledge lay the thatch. Yogis, celibates, ascetics, and renunciates came to recognize this dwelling. The Vedas and Puranas, like thirsty birds seeking devotion, kept repeating and listening to this teaching: that in home after home the glory of prem-lakshana bhakti (love-natured devotion) is proclaimed — such prem-lakshana bhakti has Vyas come to understand.

Kabirji, describing the Veda as a mere laborer, has said:

_Bani to pani bhare, charon Ved majoor._
_Karni to gara kare, rahani (Sahab) ka ghar door._
(The scriptural word only carries water; all four Vedas are but laborers. Right conduct makes the mortar, but the House of the Master lies far beyond them.)

Das Kabirji says: to build the house of the Supreme Abode, the scriptures and Puranas — the paths of karma, jnana, and yoga expressed as speech — perform the lesser task of carrying water for the labor, while all four Vedas, like hired hands, toil to assist. Right conduct makes the mortar for raising this house. But the true Supreme Abode of God lies far beyond the house built of these eighty-four lakh bodily forms — it is very slight and distant by comparison. The abode fit for our eternal, peaceful dwelling is something altogether different from this house made of the eighty-four-lakh bodily forms.

_Puran jaani Ved ki, sohat param anoop._
_Aadhi bhasha netra binu, ko lakhi paave roop._
(Das Kabirji says: the language of the Veda, taken in full, is beautiful throughout, but without the "half eye" — the understanding that guides one toward devotion — no one can perceive the form of love-devotion.)

_Bani to pani bhare, charon Ved majoor._
_Chooka, sevak bandagi, kiya chakri door._
_Chhin mein chooke chakri, to pal mein kije door._
(Das Kabirji says: the speech of the scriptures and Puranas toils hard to expound my devotion — that is, devotion to God — and the four Vedas labor hard at it too. But should any of them err in serving me, or grow careless in that service, I will dismiss them from my service at once.)

_Ved kahe main kachhu na jaanu, swasan ke sang aay._
_Daras het kar, bandagi, gun anek mein gaaya._
(Das Kabirji says: as the scripture states — "asya mahato bhutasya nihshvasitam etad yad Rig-Vedo Yajur-Vedah Sama-Vedah," this is the very breath of that great Being — so the Veda itself says: I have arisen from the breath of the Supreme Person. What is His form? How could I describe it? I know nothing of it; I only sing, in countless ways, of His qualities in the hope of glimpsing Him. The Vedas tried hard to describe the Lord's nature but could not, and in the end, exhausted, could only say of Him "not this, not this" — neti neti.)

_Bed hamara Bed hai, ham Bedon ke manhi._
_Jaun bhed mein main baasu, Bedon jaanat naahi._
_Jo maarag ham chale, so Vedon ku gam naahi._
(Das Kabirji says: hence devotees declare — the Veda is ours, and we too dwell within the Veda; but in the secret depth where we truly abide, the Veda has no knowledge. As it is said in the Taittiriya text, "yato vacho nivartante aprapya manasa saha" — that from which words, together with the mind, turn back unable to reach — such is the path of love-devotion that devotees like us have walked, a path of which the Veda has no understanding whatsoever.)

Criticizing the blindly superstitious and the religious fanatic, Kabirji says:

_Guru pashu, nar pashu naari, Ved pashu sansaar._
_Manush vaako jaaniyo, jaaka vimal vichaar._
(Das Kabirji says: in this world some foolish people are as brutish as cattle — slaves to their guru, cowed by their wives, or blindly Veda-bound. But truly, only one who discerns right from wrong, good from bad, one governed by reason, deserves to be called a real human being.)

_Nar pashu, guru pashu, Ved pashu, triya pashu sansaar._
_Kahai Kabir so pashu nahin, jaake vimal vichaar._
(Das Kabirji says: foolish people are like dull-witted cattle — some enslaved to other men, some to their guru, some unmanly and henpecked by their wives. But those who hold within themselves the discernment of right and wrong are, in the true sense, called human.)

_Balihari vah doodh ki, jaamein nikse dheev._
_Aadhi sakhi Kabir ki, char Vedka jiiye._
(Das Kabirji says: blessed is that milk — the four Vedas, the scripture of devotion — from which the ghee of Ram-nam emerges. Even half a sakhi of Kabir's carries the very life-essence of all four Vedas, since the Vedas themselves arise from that Name; thus this half-sakhi proves that Ram-nam is the origin of everything.)

_Aisa adbad jin katho, katho to raakho chhipaay._
_Bed katalbe na lakho, to kahe kaun patipaay._
(Das Kabirji says: do not declare the nature of God to be "this" or "that," as though wondrous and fully describable; and if you try, you will never manage to say it completely, for the telling will remain hidden and incomplete — who, then, would believe whatever you say?)

_Jyon paya madhya jheev hai, tyon Ramiya sab thaur._
_Kathta bakta bahut hai, math kaadhe te aur._
(Das Kabirji says: just as ghee lies within milk, so the nature of God pervades everywhere in this world. Many talk and prattle about what He is like, saying "it is this," "it is that" — but just as one churns curd to separate out its ghee, only a rare few are able to separate out the Supreme Brahman, seemingly mixed with maya, and attain the ultimate Truth.)

_Kabir, Bed Kataleb donun jug, joothi unki aash._
_Hindu Turak naarak mein padein, Vedon ku vishwaas._
(Das Kabirji says: both the Veda and the Qur'an are mistaken in expounding the nature of God and showing the path to reach Him. Both Hindus and Muslims fall into hell by placing their trust in the Veda and the Qur'an respectively.)

_Kabir, char Ved padhaayke, Harise na upajya het._
_Maal (laali) Kabira le gaye, pandit dhoonde khet._
(Das Kabirji says: though people have the four Vedas recited to them, love for devotion to God does not arise from it in the end. But whatever essential wealth of Ram-nam lay within the Vedas, the loving devotees have already taken it away. The real crop was that; and the learned pundits, after the harvest is already reaped, keep rummaging through the leftover stubble looking for grain — struggling amid the stubble of ritual, japa, austerity, and vow, searching for the genuine harvest of devotion, which is not to be found there, for the devotees have already carried it off.)

_Kabir, kathni kathe so poot hamara, Ved padhe so naati._
_Rahani rahe so guru hamara, ham rahani ke saathi._
(Das Kabirji says: those who merely speak as they please, whatever suits them, I regard as my own son, as a father keeps a son under his authority. Those who recite the Vedas, that is, perform ritual acts, I regard as my own kin — as it is said, "we are within the Veda," meaning devotees like us treat the Veda as our own servant. And those who hold within themselves the secret truth of God are my guru, my venerable saint-guru; I keep company with such secret-bearing saint-gurus, following the conduct they teach.)

_Kabir, Ved bada na Ved-si, nahi Gokul ki Brajnaar._
_Unhu sahaj paayi nahin, rahi pokaar pokaar. ||126||_
(Das Kabirji says: the Veda is not great enough to attain the Lord's love-nectar, nor can those learned in the Veda attain or bestow this supreme Truth; and even the standing of the women of Gokul, the Braj-nari, is not so great — for they did not effortlessly attain the full bliss of that love. When the circle of the rasa dance broke apart, they were left distressed and agitated, crying out in the pain of separation from the Lord.)

_Kabir, deepak joya gyaan ka, dekha aparam Dev._
_Char Ved ki gam nahin, tahan Kabira sev._
(I lit the red lamp of love-devotion and beheld the incomparable Supreme Lord. Where the speech of the four Vedas cannot reach — O Kabir, strive there for that divine Truth; practice devotion there.)

_Jot Julaho pragatchyo, kiyo naam prakaash._
_Ved mathi makhan liyo, pandit pive chhaash. ||2||_
(Maharaj Jivandasji says: a single flame arose in the form of the weaver-saint Sadguru Kabir, and he illumined the truth of God. By churning and analyzing the Vedas he attained the butter-like supreme essence of Ram-nam, while the learned pundits drank only the buttermilk — the recitation of Vedas and rituals, empty of the essence of God.)

_Ved van man Jeevna, bhoolya sab sansaar._
_Karam dharam phaansi bhayi, Kaazi Brahman kaal._
(Maharaj Jivandasji says: in the wilderness-forest of the Veda, O Jivan, the whole world has lost its way. Rituals, japa, and austerity have become like a noose, and Qazis and Brahmins have become the executioners who tighten it, agents of destruction.)

_Ved-Kabed doy haathiya, Kaazi Brahman maath._
_Tinke sir par Sevda, tahan na Kabira jaat._
(Das Kabirji says: the Veda and the Qur'an have become like two grasping hands holding worldly people fast, and the Qazis and Brahmins have become the authorities gripping us in those two hands. Worse still are the Sevadas — Jain monks who let their hair grow uncut, like sorcerers — so the community of Kabir's devotees will have nothing to do with them.)

_Kabir, Kaazi padhe Quran ku, pandit Ved Puraan._
_Taake peechhe sab jug chalya, e dozakh ka agwaan._
(Das Kabirji says: the Qazis recite the Qur'an, and the pundits read the Vedas and Puranas. The whole world follows behind them, acting as they say — thus these people are the leaders who take us down into hell.)

_Ajahun tera sab mite, jo guru-mukh paave bhed._
_Pandit paas na baithiye, baithi na suniye Ved._
(Das Kabirji says: even now, all your doubt can be dispelled if you receive the teaching of the true nature through the mouth of the Guru; but do not sit near Vedic pundits, and do not listen to their empty, wordy expositions of the Veda. Reference: R.ji 256/2, p. 603.)

_Vede bhoolya sakal jug, toon nahin apne saath._
_Took took karun Jeevna, jo chadhe hamare haath._
(Maharaj Jivandasji says: O Veda, you have led the whole world astray and deceived it, but you cannot come along with those of us who hold love-devotion — we will not keep you with us. But if you should ever fall into our grasp, O Jivan, I will tear you to pieces.)

_Bed bhed jaanai nahin, neti neti kahai bain._
_Ta Mohan son Radhika, kahai mahaavar dain._
(Devotees possessed of prem-lakshana bhakti neither know nor care for the convoluted commands of the Veda. To the Veda's teaching of ritual, japa, and austerity, such lovers keep saying, "we will not accept this, we will not do that" — even as the Veda itself, regarding the nature of God, can only keep saying "not this, not that." That very God, Shri Krishna, whom the Veda cannot capture, Radhikaji has brought so completely under her sway that she commands Him, "apply red lac-dye to the soles of my feet.")

_Kabir, Ram kaha tin sab laha, lahe safal shastra ka bhed._
_Ram na kahe so narke gaya, padhte charon Ved._
(Das Kabirji says: those who took the Name of Ram gained everything — they grasped the very essence of all the scriptures. Those who did not chant the Name of Ram had to go to hell, even though they recited all four Vedas.)

_Gharti to haandi bhayi, dhakkan bhaya aakash._
_Char Ved kaathi bhayi, jeev ka kahan nikaash._
(Das Kabirji says: this earth has become like a cooking pot in which the soul is trapped and made to suffer, and the sky above it has become its lid, while the four Vedas have become the firewood beneath it. In such a state of suffering, from where can this soul ever find its release, ever escape from that pot?)

_Kabir, dharti to haandi sahi, dhaapan sahi aakash._
_Guru (shabda) prataape bhakti pachha payi, jeev ka tahan nikaash._
(Das Kabirji says: let it be that the earth is like a pot and the sky its lid — that is no matter. But if, by the grace of the Guru's teaching, we attain love-devotion, then through it the soul will find its deliverance.)

In this world, the earth made of the eighty-four lakh bodies through which birth and death occur is that pot, and delusion (maya) is its lid; within it the four Vedas, in their fourfold form, torment this soul with the fire of rituals, japa, and austerity as though it were firewood. But the Guru shows us the way and means to escape from this bondage of worldly existence by teaching us devotion to Ram-nam, so that we may gain release.

_Ved mein bahu bhed hai, jaane virla koy._
_Sundar Sadguru mila vina, nirvaaro na hoy._
(Sundardas says: the Veda holds within it many hidden layers of meaning that only a rare few can know; unless, O Sundar, one finds a true Sadguru, deliverance from its deceptive snares cannot be attained.)

The Veda has been regarded as a servant — "we are within the Veda" means we have accepted the Veda in the capacity of a servant. If a servant errs, the master does not accept it and dismisses him; likewise, when the Veda, instead of prompting love-devotion, imposes only the contrary work of ritual, devotees do not accept it. Since the Veda's commands, bound up as they are with the three gunas, would break the wholehearted devotion required of devotees, they are not acceptable to that extent, and to that extent the Veda must be opposed — but this does not mean that the Veda disrespects devotion to God; rather, it has simply been granted the standing of a servant to the devotees. Nana Parekh, in the raga Velaval, has written beautifully of the Veda:

_Saheb mere Saiyan, vinti karun tohi._
_Ketik vaata atapati, samjhaavo mohi. (tek)_
_Bhai re Ved bada sab ko kahai, Hari mukh the aaya._
_Gopijan peechhe dharya, param pad paaya. ||1||_
_Bhai re Shukdev samaran kiya, maaya sab tyaagi._
_Vaikunth pedhan na diya, meri daajh na bhaagi. ||2||_
_Bhai re Parath ke tum saarthi, mohe achraj aave._
_Aisa bhagat ekaantka, Himaale kyun jaave. ||3||_
_Bhai re Aadhav Akrur aadhdehi, jan nikat kahaaya._
_Aise Harijan dekhtaan, shankh supach bajaaya. ||4||_
_Bhai re akath katha behad ki, boojhe mat mohi._
_Nana Sadguru bina mile, cheene nahin koi. ||5||_
(O Lord, my Master, I plead with You: many things about You leave me puzzled — explain them and grant me understanding. Everyone says the Veda is the greatest, that it came from Your own mouth and is uncreated; yet the gopis set aside its commands and still attained the Supreme Abode. Shukadev renounced all pleasure for knowledge and detachment, yet without love-devotion he was kept from entering Your Abode, and this grief has never left me. I marvel that You became the charioteer of Arjuna, Your own devoted soul, and yet he went to the Himalayas hoping to ascend to heaven. In the presence of Your closest devotees such as Uddhava and Akrura, it was an outcaste's conch that was sounded at the Rajasuya sacrifice. O Lord, of whom nothing can truly be said and who is without limit, no one can fully understand You; without a true Sadguru, says Nana the Vaishnav, no one can know how to love You, nor grasp Your wonders.)

Having quoted the sakhi "Ved hamare het hai" — the Veda works for our benefit — the nature of the path of karma laid down by the Veda has thus been explained through Kabir's sakhis. The following section now turns to exclusive, one-pointed devotion. A servant (kinkar) must observe due deference toward his master; but if the master instead defers to the servant, he would be counted a fool, an utter fool. In the same way, since the Veda is the servant, it is the Veda that must defer to the devotee, its true master — but should the devotee defer to the Veda instead, he would be counted an utter fool. Regarding this it is said:

_Bhane besi bhookho uthe, chaakarni raakhe maazha._
_Dharni baaydithi sharmaay, te murakhno raja._
(One who sits down to eat and rises still hungry, one who defers to his own servant, and one who is bashful before his own wife — such a person is the very king of fools.)

Ghost-Offerings (Pret Bhojan) and the Exclusive Devotee — pret bhojan is reckoned as company kept with Shakta and Salil worshippers. Once, in the Garuda Purana, what Shri Krishna said about pret bhojan is set out in verse 57:

_Varam halaahalam bhakshyam kaakamamsam shunastatha._
_Shvapachasya-annam bhunkshya pretabhojanam aatyaja. ||57||_
(Better to eat deadly poison, better to eat the flesh of a crow or a dog, better to eat food from an outcaste's house — but abandon pret bhojan, food offered to the dead, altogether.)

Garuda, son of Vinata, is the Lord's own carrier; only by eating pure food does he remain fit to carry Him.

_Hari-bhakti-vihitanam samsargo naraka-pradah._
_Udakam tu suraapaanam, annam gomamsa-sannibham._
(Association with those devoid of devotion to God leads to hell; the water in their house is like liquor, and their food is like forbidden cow's flesh.)

_Sant pade so langhna, aan-dasha nahin jaay._
_Jo kabahu bhookha rahai, ananya ke ghar paay. ||13||_
(The Vaishnav Nana Parekh, in the Sant Ang, says: even should a saintly devotee have to fast for a hundred days, he will not fall into wretchedness for it. If ever a time of hunger comes, he would rather stay hungry than eat — he will eat only in the house of an exclusive devotee.)

The Lord tells Garuda: by eating pret bhojan, tens of millions upon tens of millions of our births are ruined. What is to be counted as pret bhojan is described in verse 58:

_Deva-yajnaam deva-havyaam anya-devam-upaashritaah._
_Ekaadashyaam cha dvaadashyaam pretabhojyaath. ||58||_
(Food connected with sacrifices, oblations, and the worship of other deities, or eaten at the eleventh- or twelfth-day death rites, is pret bhojan, and it destroys the merit of one who partakes.)

Food from a yajna, homa, or havan; food offered to another deity; food from one not entitled to wear tilak and tulsi and who does not wear them; and food from the eleventh- or twelfth-day death rites — all these are counted as pret bhojan. Food offered before an image should not be eaten — from the commentary on the Parashar Smriti, chapter 11: scripture forbids eating food cooked and offered to deities in temples; only those of great austerity may eat it. Nowadays many people, thinking temple prasad sacred, eat it gladly, but the scriptures forbid eating food offered before images of deities. Food offered to Vishnu is counted pure, but only when worshipped within a private household shrine; in public temples, scripture forbids eating the food offered before the images, and whoever eats it incurs sin. It is also said in the Anusmriti:

_Samvatsarena patati patitena sahaacharan._
_Yaajanaadhyaapanaayaunaatraatu yaanaasanaashanaat._
(A man becomes fallen who, for a full year, travels in the same vehicle with a fallen person, sits on the same seat, or eats in the same row with him; but by officiating his sacrifices, teaching him, or exchanging daughters in marriage with him, one becomes fallen at once.)

Discussing pret bhojan, the Samagam gives this sakhi of Kabirji:

_Kabir, hom kanagat kaarto, saakut raandhyo khaay._
_Jeevat vishta shwaan ki, mooye narak le jaay._
(Das Kabirji says: one who eats food from homa, havan, shraddha rites, from the eleventh-day death feast, or food cooked by a Shakta, is, while still living, as impure as a dog's filth, and after death Yama's messengers carry him off to hell.)

Those who eat the food of the twelfth- or thirteenth-day death rites are counted of low standing, and Brahmins who do so are counted among them. Its sakhi:

_Brahman Bhangi ek hai, unki ek hi jaat._
_Vo kafan ko let hai, o teraahme khaat._
(The Brahmin and the sweeper are, in this respect, one and the same kind: the sweeper takes the burial shroud, while the Brahmin eats the food of the twelfth- and thirteenth-day rites.)

_Brahman Bhangi Rawka, chautha kahiye kaag._
_Kahe Kabir e chaaron janka, murda upar laag._
(Das Kabir says: Brahmins, sweepers, Rawal beggars, and, fourth, crows — all four keep watch over a corpse, ever ready to consume what belongs to the dead.)

Improper eating and drinking ruins one's reputation, and this is why Brahmins become disgraced. Its sakhi:

_Aambo phal pat raakhke, mahu phale pat khoye._
_Vaako paani je piye, tahan pat kahan te hoye._
(The mango fruit keeps one's honor intact, but whoever drinks the liquor made from mahua fruit — how can his honor be preserved?)

In this way, one who eats improperly loses his reputation, while one who eats and lives properly is highly valued. Food offered to another deity is of the lowest order, while food offered to God is the highest. It is said in the Gautami Tantra:

_Tulasi-dala-maatrena jalasya chulukena cha._
_Vikrinita svam-aatmaanam bhaktebhyo bhakta-vatsalah._
(The Lord is so compassionate and so affectionate toward His devotees that He gives away His very own Self to them for the price of a single tulsi leaf and a palmful of water offered with devotion.)

_Kabir, prasaad sohi kijiye, Hari arpit hoye._
_Aur bhojan nakhod hai, kahet Kabira soy._
(Das Kabirji says: one should take as prasad only what has been offered to God; all other food, say Kabir and the saints, is inauspicious.)

_Bin arpan bhojan kare, bin arpan jal paan._
_Bin arpan sumaran kare, ehi pret samaan._
(Whoever eats food, drinks water, or even remembers God without first offering it to Him — that act is counted as base as pret bhojan.)

In verse 59 of the Samagam, the same warning that the Lord gave Garuda about pret bhojan is given to exclusive Vaishnav devotees:

_Mrutakasya paavakash-chaiva shaaktasya mandire._
_Jalam pitvaa suraapaanam, annam gomaamsa bhakshanam. ||59||_
(Better to cook one's food with fire brought from a funeral pyre than to bring even an ember from a Shakta's house; water from a Shakta's house is as forbidden as liquor, and food from there is as inedible as cow's flesh.)

Shakta people consider impure whatever they dislike and pure whatever they like:

_Angamtu apavitra gani, gamtu ganyun pavitra._
_Chudo na ganyu haadku, jagat vichaar vichitra._
(Self-interested people consider impure whatever displeases them, and pure whatever pleases them — as when ivory bangles, though made of bone, are still counted an essential ornament for married women. Such is the strange, contradictory nature of such people.)

People regard women's natural monthly courses as unclean, while they regard the slaughter of animals in sacrifices, meat-eating, and the intoxicating drink of soma as sacred. People of such twisted, contrary inclination are as base as butchers, and association with such Shakta worshippers is therefore to be avoided. The Samagam advises staying far from such people, and how deeply wicked they are is stated in this fifty-ninth verse: it is better to cook with fire brought from a burning corpse in the cremation ground than to bring fire even from a Shakta's house, for that brings fault and sin upon us. It is said that fire itself is never tainted by what it touches, since fire reduces everything to ash — yet even so, we are commanded to stay far from the very fire kept in such a wicked person's house. Prescribing restrictions regarding Shakta and Salil worshippers, the Samagam gives seven sakhis:

_Kabir, Saakut keri sabha rachi, tahan jan baithan jaay._
_Ek gohaade kyun bane, rojh gadha aur gaay. ||1||_
(Das Kabirji says: devotees do not go to sit in the assembly of Shakta people, for just as chaos would come of penning wild nilgai, donkeys, and cows together in one enclosure, the same wretched fate would befall devotees there. People of every disposition — rajasic, tamasic, and sattvic — gather there and quarrel, and in such conditions the Lord's devotees are put to great difficulty.)

Shakta people worship other deities; Salil people keep a foot on both sides, worshipping both their chosen deity (ishta-dev) and other deities; but exclusive devotees acknowledge none other than their ishta-dev. Hence, in the quarrels between Shaktas and Salils, they are made to suffer.

_Kabir, had ke jeevsan, hit kari mukhai na bol._
_Jo laage behad son, tinson kachhu kachhu bol. ||2||_
(Das Kabirji says: O devotee, do not, out of affection, discuss the inner matters of love-devotion with those still bound within the limits of social convention and caste propriety; but with those who have left behind family custom and caste convention and become absorbed in love-devotion to the Supreme Being, speak freely and lovingly of devotion.)

_Kabir, had rahe so maanvi, behad rahe so saadh._
_Had behad se jo koi nyaara, taaka matta agaadh. ||3||_
(Das Kabirji says: "had," the bound, means one who performs the duties of caste and station strictly as the Veda prescribes — an ordinary human being; "behad," beyond bound, means one who rejects those duties entirely and follows the path of yoga — a sadhak. And those who dwell on the path of love-devotion, distinct from both the path of knowledge and the path of ritual action, hold a principle whose depth is beyond measure.)

_Mukh se rahe so maanvi, man se rahe so dev._
_Surat se rahe so sant hai, vidh jaano bhev._
(One who repeats the Name only with the mouth is merely a man; one who repeats it with the mind is like an exalted celestial; and one who repeats it with the inner attention is a saint — understand thus the mystery of such repetition.)

_Sant saath bahu antara, jyon dharti aakash._
_Sant chaahe Ramku, saadh santki aash._
(Das Kabirji says: there is a very great difference between the Sant and the sadhak — as great as the distance between earth and sky. Sants desire to attain God, Ram, directly, while sadhaks desire above all to attain a true Sant, since only through finding one does their own practice bear fruit.)

_Kabir, had mein Ram na paaiya, behad hai bharpoor._
_Had behad ki gam nahi, taasu Ram hazoor._
(Das Kabirji says: God is not attained within the bounds of caste convention and Vedic custom; He is found in full only beyond those bounds. One who has passed beyond all concern with either bound or unbound stands in the very presence of Ram.)

Devotion could not be attained through the limits of social custom and Vedic convention; one who breaks through those limits gains deep, direct experience. That state which lies beyond every limit — attained by one who breaks past social shame and pride to sound the banner of devotion — reveals the divine Truth to him directly.

_Kabisa, saadhu bahu antara, jyun dharti brahmaand._
_Saadhu odhaare aapku, sant odhaare khand._
(Das Kabirji says: there is a very great difference between sadhaks — knowers, meditators, yogis — and Sants, as great as the distance between earth and sky in their work. For sadhus practice for their own individual benefit, while Sants are well-wishers striving for the welfare of the whole universe — as the saying goes, "udaracharitanam vasudhaiva kutumbakam," for the noble-hearted the whole world is one family.)

Regarding the sadhu, Maharaj Gyaniji says:

_Mankun saadhe saadh so, raakho Saheb maanhi._
_Gyaani doojaa bhekh sab, saadh kahaave naahi. ||41||_
(Maharaj Gyaniji says: only those who strive to master the mind and keep their disposition fixed on God are true sadhaks; all others, he says, are mere costume-wearers, and cannot be called true sadhus or saints.)

_Saakutasu Jeevna, het kari mukhahi na bole._
_Salil bhagatsu munagrah, aninsu antar khol. ||5||_
(Sadguru Maharaj Jivandasji says: O Jivan, do not exchange loving words with Shakta people, nor deal warmly with them; keep your relations with Salil devotees firmly closed off. But with the exclusive, single-minded devotee, open your heart freely, without reservation or discrimination, and deal with him wholeheartedly.)

Trikamdas Gordhandas has composed a linked verse (kundali) upon this sakhi:

_Saakutansu Jeevna, tun het kari mukhahi na bol._
_Salil bhagatsu maun grah, aninsun antar khol._
_Anin sun antar bol, bol guru-mukh vaani._
_Salil Saakut sang chhod, bhataksho chaaro khaani._
_Kahun chhun vagaadi dhol, saambhale shishya Sadguru tana._
_Tun het kari mukh hi na bol, Saakutansun Jeevna._
(O Jivan, do not speak lovingly with your own mouth to the Shakta; keep silence toward the Salil devotee, but open your heart to the exclusive one. Open your heart to the exclusive devotee, and speak only the words that come through the Guru's own mouth; leave the company of both Salil and Shakta, or you will wander through all four species of birth. I proclaim this beating the drum, that the disciples of the Sadguru may hear it: do not speak lovingly with your own mouth to the Shakta, O Jivan.)
